The Boot of Death
German Campaign: 1943-1945
Campaign designer: Pablo Schelgel, 2004

After the defeat of the Africa Korps the next step for the Allies was the invasion of Sicily and the Italian mainland, hoping to force the surrender of this German allied and open a second front in Europe. They were expecting a quick victory and the retreat of the German army towards the Alps, but situation turned into a bloody conflict that lasted until the end of war.
This campaign reflects the true historical battles in which the German Army fought bravely.

On the first day of the campaign the Leibstandarte had achieved almost all its objectives.  By the evening of the 1st, the bulk of the Regiment was across the river and ready to advance on Wieuroszov, where it would link up with the 17th Infantry Division.  This was accomplished, and in the early hours of the next morning, the Leibstandarte advanced towards Burzenin, where it received orders to cross the Warta River.
Fall Weiss - September 1st, 1939
Prosna River Crossing

The Leibstandarte had been preparing for the Polish campaign since June, and in August had recieved orders to move from their Lichterfelde Barracks to an assembly area in East Berlin. The OKW remained sceptical of SS combat abilities, yet had little option but to accept Hitler's wish that the SS be involved in the attack.

LSSAH was attached to XIII Corps, 8th Armee, Army Group South, with the task of defending the left flank of 10th Armee.  In the initial advance the Leibstandarte - a fully motorised unit - was put under the control of the 17th Infantry Division and was assigned the task of forward reconnaissance and the defence of slower moving units.

The first objective for the LSSAH was to cross the Prosna River and assualt the anti-tank guns across the bridge.  They would then move quickly to seize the heights, and move into the village of Boleslavecz.  They were able to hold the village despite fierce counter-attacks by three Polish infantry divisions and cavalry elements.
Well done Comrade, you've got the control of Metz, Comrade Stalin is glad with your work.

With the route to Warsaw now wide open, the 10th Army turned its axis of advance north and advanced toward the capital from the south-west, while the 4th Army closed from the north.  Guderian's armoured corps linked up with von Kleist's armoured corps at Brest-Litovsk on the 14th, effectively cutting off any potential escape route.

On the Western approaches the 1st Battalion of the Leibstandarte fought bitterly to wrest Oltarzev from its stubborn defenders.  The Pole's although battered, were far from beaten and had declared Warsaw a fortress city.  Instead of withdrawing east, they began a retreat south-east and struck at the 8th Army.  The attacks temporarily threw the Germans off balance and the Leibstandarte was forced onto the defensive.

At this point in the campaign the Leibstandarte was able to link up with the 9th Panzer Division in the drive to Rotterdam.  Despite the fact that German airborne troops held the vital Maas bridge at Moerdijk, the tenacious Dutch defence in the north of the city had thus far prevented a crossing.  Hitler issued an ultimatum to the Dutch - capitulate or Rotterdam would be bombed.  Despite ongoing negotiations, the Luftwaffe attacked the city, citing a breakdown in communications.

Following the air raid, on the 13th of May, the Leibstandarte advanced through Rotterdam and was involved in an incident which drew heavy criticism from the army.  After spotting Dutch soldiers loitering outside a building, soldiers of the LSSAH opened fire.  Inside that building Dutch and German officers were negotiating a surrender.  One of the German officers inside was Airborne Commander Karl Student, who was severely wounded by the assault.
For the army, it was proof again of the indiscipline of the Waffen SS.

After the seizure of the Wattenberg heights, the Leibstandarte doggedly pursued the retreating enemy.  The 2nd Battalion tasked with capturing the town of Wormhoudt, encoutered stiff resistance from men of the British 48th Infantry Division, and on 28th May the town was still held by British forces.  As the fighting continued, a number of the 4th Chesire Regiment were taken prisoner and led to a barn, which was then raked with machine gun fire.  Grenades were then tossed inside, and by the time an officer had halted the slaughter, 65 of the 80 POW's were dead.  Those who survived this incident have since implicated Wilhelm Mohnke as the officer who gave the execution order.

Dietrich however was cleared of any wrong doing, having spent the day in a muddy ditch after coming under fire from some isolated British soldiers.  With his car on fire, he and his companions took shelter in the ditch, where the Leibstandarte commander covered himself in damp mud to protect against the burning petrol of his car.

The Leibstandarte briefly rested after the fall of Dunkirk, and then moved south with Von Kleist's armoured group where it took part in some minor actions.  The campaign in France cost the Leibstandarte some 500 casualties.  The unit was amply rewarded for its performance and in August was upgraded to Brigade status and began training for Operation Sealion - the proposed invasion of Britain.

After taking Skopje, the Leibstandarte turned soouth, and headed for the strategically important Monastir Gap - the gateway to Greece.  The reconnaissance battalion of the Leibstandarte that had been sent ahead did not encounter any strong opposition until it reached the area east of Florina. Against all expectations, the enemy had left open the Monastir Gap. The Germans did not hesitate to exploit their advantage and continued the advance in the direction of Kozani.

The Leibstandarte was instrumental in preventing any Soviet breakout's during the encirclement, as the Soviets threw armour, cavalry and scores of infantry in their direction.  Each time the division was able to repel these attacks, and for its efforts the Leibstandarte earned considerable praise from corps commander, Generalmajor Kempf.  The encirclement was completed on the 8th of August when the 6th Army met the 17th Army on the Southern Bug River, trapping two whole Soviet armies and a large part of another.
The troops in the pocket were finally eliminated on 22nd August, but the focus of the Leibstandarte's advance had already shifted towards the industrial centre of Kherson.

At Dubno, the Leibstandarte was able to defeat the Soviet counter-attack and prevent them from cutting the lengthening line of communications.  Victory came at a cost however, as the division lost 683 killed and wounded.  Following the battle, von Kleist and his armoured group were able to breakthrough the Stalin Line east of Zhitomir, driving a wedge between two Soviet armies.  Moving in behind this breakthrough, the division quickly sped along the road to Kiev, where it soon found itself thrown onto the backfoot thanks to a wide-ranging Soviet attack on the Southwest front.

When the Soviet attacks halted, Hitler's gaze fixed onto Uman, a major transport hub for the Crimea, which had the added attraction of encircling the Soviet forces holding up the 17th and 18th armies.

Comrade, this is the last step to conquer Romans's Motherland. We've watched some allied ships approaching, so submarines and extra reinforcements are on the way.

Only after bitter and bloody fighting were the Leibstandarte able to capture Bubry and the road junction at Sasselje.  Arriving at Kherson on the 17th of August, the division fought yet another bitter battle through the streets for three days before the defenders finally fled the city.

Rostov was fully taken on the 21st November.  In its part in the attack the Leibstandarte had captured the main railway bridge intact, earning SS-Haupsturmfuhrer Heinrich Springer the Knights Cross.  Von Kleist's armour was able to pour over this vital crossing point and play a pivotal role in the victory.  For the division came the reward of 10,000 prisoners, 159 artillery pieces, 56 tanks and 2 armoured trains.

After five days of bitter fighting, the SS-Panzer Corps reached the city of Kharkov.  Three more days of viscious fighting throughout the city followed, and the city was secured on the 14th March.  On the 18th, Byelgorod was retaken, thus regaining the defensive line of the Donets to Byelgorod, and correcting the tactical situation brought about by the Stalingrad disaster.

The battle of Kharkov cost the Leibstandarte 167 officers, 4,373 NCOs and soldiers - 44 percent of its fighting strength.  The square in Kharkov was renamed 'Leibstandarteplatz' in the division's honour, and on March 21st, Hitler awarded Dietrich the Swords to his Knights Cross.
The late spring on the Eastern Front was quiet, a respite that afforded the division vital needed time for rest and refitting.

On the 12th, the Soviet Guards Tank Army launched a series of uncoordinated strikes with the intention to seperate the SS divisions.  In an area of only a few square miles, firing at almost point-blank range across the dust-choked plain, the superior German tank guns counted for nothing against suicidal attacks by Soviet tank crews.  In the heavy fighting that ensued the heavy company of the Leibstandarte's tank regiment engaged and destroyed the Soviet 181st Tank Regiment, without loss.  On both sides however, losses were high.  At the end of the day a thick pall of smoke hung over the battlefield.

The Soviet attack had been driven off, but at a heavy price, and the SS-Panzer Corps now held the area around Prokhorovka and the railroad.  In the north however, the Soviets had launched a strong counter-attack behind the 9th Army, threatining them with encirclement - forcing General Model to halt his advance, and pull back his forces.  With the situation in the north becoming increasingly precarious, Hitler called 'Zitadelle' off on the 13th July.
At Kursk the Leibstandarte paid heavily - 2,753 casaulties, including 474 dead, and 19 tanks lost.  Following the Kursk campaign, the Leibstandarte was sent to Italy for occupation duty.

Zhitomir was taken, and although it would soon have to be relinquished, Soviet supply routes between the city and Kiev were cut.  The Leibstandarte moved on Brusilov, where it met a strong concentration of 5th and 8th Guards Armoured Corps, and 1st Guard Cavalry Corps.  With the 1st and 9th Panzer Divisions attacking the northern and southern flanks, and Leibstandarte from the west, on 24th November the concentration was encircled and destroyed.  On 16th December amid biting cold and blinding snowstorms the division advanced east with the 1st and 7th Panzer divisions from Korosten, aiming at encircling the Soviet armies around Meleni.  This was achieved, but with so few troops that the positions could not be held and soon attack turned to retreat.

As the year drew to a close, the 4th Panzer Army was pushed back west and south of the city by a fresh offensive launched on Christmas Eve by the combined forces of four Soviet armies plus two independent corps against the southern rim of Kiev.  The next day it developed a second thrust west, which threatened to destroy the entire left flank of Army Group South, and succeeded in recapturing Zhitomir and the road linking it to Kiev.  While recognising that this thrust could be employed to drive the two army groups back against the Black Sea and Carpathian Mountains, Hitler saw that the southern attack posed the danger of an envelopment of Army Group South and A between the Dniepr and Dniestr Rivers, and considered it the greatest danger.

Caen had been lost, and the Leibstandarte had fallen back to the Bourgebus ridge, where they held the line and inflicted heavy casaulties upon the British 7th and 11th Armoured Divisions.  However, the weakened German defences began to lose the battle of attrition, with few reinforcements arriving, and roaming Allied bombers destroying supplies before the could reach the lines.  The division now helped to hold the Caen-Falaise highway until the end of July against repeated British attacks.

In the last week of July, the US forces had launched a breakout attempt which pulled them out of the bocage country and into the open countryside.  Hitler ordered a counter-attack, of which the Leibstandarte was to be part of, aimed at Avranches and St. Lo which failed.  Subsequently a Canadian attack which thrust south-west threatened to envelop the German forces, and the LSSAH was pulled back into defensive positions.

The Leibstandarte attack was eventually thwarted by blown bridges and a stubborn defence by the American troops.  By December 23rd, the division was being pushed back following its intial success.  Kampfgruppe Peiper, isolated and under heavy attacks at Stoumont, was given permission to break out to the east while the rest of the division provided cover.  Leaving behind 150 U.S. prisoners and some wounded to destroy his remaining tanks, Peiper led his battered and weary troops back to German lines.
KG Peiper started the attack with 5,800 men, and left with just 800 survivors.

On the day of the German offensive snow was falling from low cloud and the temperature hovered on either side of zero degrees celcius.  The Leibstandarte began its attack at 0430 hours with an artillery barrage against the 68th Guards Rifle Division positions.  The Soviet defences were strong and well prepared, and the Leibstandarte lost a number of tanks to mines and flame-throwers.  Despite the shock of finding the Soviets well prepared, the Leibstandarte broke through, and by March 14th had reached Simontoya, securing a bridgehead over the Sio Canal by the 15th.  By this point however, the corps left flank was badly exposed, prompting Dietrich to recommend a retreat to defensive positions, as further advance was impossible, owing to the hilly, broken and wooded terrain.

Soviet attacks across the Sarvis and Sio Canals were seen as an ominous sign of things to come.  It was clear from intelligence reports that the Soviets were attempting to cut off the Sixth Panzer Army.  On the 16th two Soviet armies launched a major attack between Szekesfehervar and the Vertes hills to the north.  By the 18th, the LSSAH was given orders to withdraw from Simontoya, thus ending the divisions last offensive action of the war.

For the rescue attempt von Manstein concentrated most of his tank strength in the 46th and 3rd Panzer Corps, and attached Leibstandarte to the latter.  On 11th February the breakout began, with Leibstandarte attacking on the northern flank with the 1st, 17th and 16th Panzer Divisions assaulting to the south.  Conditions could not have been worse with thick fog and hevaily bogged roads rendering rapid movement impossible.  Zhukov threw in the 5th Guards Tank Army to counter the German thrust and halted the Northern flank when it was barely eight miles from the trapped pocket.  Realising that the link-up he envisaged had failed, Hitler consented to a break-out attempt on 16th February, and that night a slow-moving column formed.  Leaving behind the wounded and most of their equipment, 35,000 men began moving toward 3rd Panzer Corps positions.  Men, of the Leibstandarte, covering the retreat, showed considerable bravery.  In one documentated incident, two NCO's of the 2nd Panzergrenadier Regiment held off two companies of Soviet troops before they could be relieved.  In all 32,000 troops had escaped, half of the forces that had been initially trapped.

In early March, the weakened divisions of von Manstein were smashed by a mighty assault by the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Ukrainian Fronts between the Carpathian mountains and the Pripet marshes.  The Leibstandarte, fighting as part of the 24th Panzer Corps, was unable to stem the tide and by the 15th was all but annihilated - less than 1,250 men remained.  In the last week of the month, together with 4th Panzer Army it was encircled at Kamenets-Podolski.  The remains of the Leibstandarte fought out of the pocket and by mid-April had reached German lines.

As the war in the east entered its fourth year, Zhukov's 1st Ukrainian Front moved across the Dnieper against Kirovgrad, taking advantage of the now severely weakened Army Group South right flank.  Two days later Kirovgrad was in Soviet hands, despite spirited defence by 11 German divisions.  Fighting a continuing series of defensive engagements in the area around Zhitomir, Korosten and Beredichev, the Leibstandarte at Beredichev was able to temporarily check the Soviet advance.  By mid-January the Soviet 1st Tank Army, spearheading 1st Ukrainian Front's southern advance, had gained 65 miles and was approaching Uman.  In knee-deep mud, sleet and blizzards, Army Group South fought desperately to prevent it's front from collapsing.

A new attack, begun on 25th January by Konev's 2nd Ukrainian Front, in four days linked up with Vatunin's 1st Ukrainian Front and encircled 6 German divisions at Korsun-Shevchenkovsky, north-west of Cherkassy.  Hitler refused to countenance any breakout attempt, insisting that von Manstein instead link up with the trapped forces and thus re-eastablish the Dniepr Line.

The cutting off of the Greek withdrawal to the south was accomplished by 20 April, following a pitched battle in the 5,000 foot high Metsovon Pass in the Pindus Mountains. Realizing the hopelessness of the situation, the Greek commander offered to surrender his army, which then consisted of fourteen divisions. After brief negotiations, which, on strict orders from Hitler, were kept secret from the Italians, the surrender was accepted with honorable terms for the defeated. In recognition of the valor with which the Greek troops had fought, their officers were permitted to retain their side arms. The soldiers were not treated as prisoners of war and were allowed to go home after the demobilization of their units.
On the 28th the remaining British forces in Greece surrendered.  During the campaign the Leibstandarte had lost 93 killed, 225 wounded and 3 missing, and thus was afforded a few days rest.

On 18th April the division was sent to France for rest and refitting, to counter the expected summer invasion of north-west Europe.  From the 25th it was headquartered at Turnhout, Belgium, as one of the elements of Dietrichs newly created I SS-Panzer Corps which was given the title Leibstandarte Adolf Hitler.  Here over 2,000 troops were transferred into the division from the 12th SS Division, and on the 3rd May Hitler decreed new equipment for the division, much of it to come straight from the factory.  With these and other replacements, by June 1944 the Leibstandarte had been rebuilt to a strength of 20,000.

Thanks to the movement sanctions imposed by Hitler on the German forces on the Western Front, the Leibstandarte was not immediately able to respond to the Allied landings on June 6th.  This left the 21st Panzer, Panzer Lehr and 12th SS Panzer Divisions to bear the brunt of the Allied assaults in the early stages of the battle for Caen.  Not until 28th of June were elements of the Leibstandarte - the 1st Panzergrenadier Regiment - able to arrive at Caen.

Operation Sudwind - February 17th, 1945

By 1945 the Leibstandarte had been successfully moved east by train to Vienna, and the difficult task of rebuilding the division began.  The situation for Germany was critical - Budapest had fallen after a 51 day seige; Warsaw, Lodz and Krakow had fallen; a Soviet Army was in East Prussia; the Red Army was now a mere 200km from Prague, and worst of all, it had crossed the river Oder, and was only 70km from Berlin.  The I SS Panzer Corps was to be used to rectify this critical situation.

The Soviets held a considerable bridgehead over the Gran river, north of Eztergom.  This position was seen as a potential assembly area for a possible thrust towards Vienna and as such it had to be elminated before the main offensive - aimed at elimating the Soviet units from the area west of the Danube and north of the Drava rivers and to secure the Nagykanizsa oil deposits - could begin.  This peliminary operation was given the code-name South Wind.

Despite widespread flooding and poor road conditions caused by an early thaw, Sudwind began at 0500 hours on the 17th of February.  Leaving high ground on their right flank and with the Gran river on their left, the Germans attacked across open, rolling, agricultural land with few villages and no serious obstacles.

By the first day, the Leibstandarte and the attached 46th Infantry Division had broken through the Soviet defences, advancing 10km.  On both the right and left flanks however, the 44th and 211th Infantry Divisions ran into strong resistance.  By the 21st, the I SS Panzer Corps had cleared the Gran bridgehead, sending the Soviets into a retreat across the Gran river.  Hitler quickly ordered that the Leibstandarte be freed as soon as possible for his next offensive, in the Lake Balaton area.
